visual_correlations.explanation: The comment is directly referencing Lewis Loflin, who is visible in Frame 2 and the context of connecting MOSFETs in parallel matches with the title of the book 'Connect MOFETS in Parallel' mentioned in the frame.
visual_correlations.comment: The speaker Lewis Loflin began by explaining how the common problem of connecting MOSFETs in parallel lies in the oftentimes neglected Cgs, or capacitance gate source, which is also connected in parallel when MOSFETs are connected in parallel. As a result, the capacitance adds up as capacitors in parallel do. In turn, the increased capacitance disrupts the drive signal. Additionally, with enhancement mode MOSFETs, they are always off until the gate action turns them on. Turning the I/O pin to MOSFETs on and off will result in a charge and discharge curve in the output voltage waveform, which ultimately causes the unexpected circuit behavior many witness in experiments.

visual_correlations.explanation: Direct reference to Lewis Loflin's connection of MOSFETs in parallel, matching Frame 2 and Frame 3, with specific details about capacitor control and waveforms from the video.
visual_correlations.comment: Connecting mosfets in parallel circuit that he has built, and I do not think I have heard of a gate operated capacitor. Parallel capacitors add together, so this has to be controlled. He shows the charts on how the wave forms are choppy then smoothed out. But reducing his turn on and turn off capacitance to smooth everything out. Slowing down the discharge surge by using a diode and resistor that looks really similar to what we have reviewed in class.

visual_correlations.explanation: The comment does not mention any visual content shown in these frames, but rather discusses MOSFETs and their behavior.
visual_correlations.comment: The speaker Lewis Loflin began by explaining how the common problem of connecting MOSFETs in parallel lies in the oftentimes neglected Cgs, or capacitance gate source, which is also connected in parallel when MOSFETs are connected in parallel. As a result, the capacitance adds up as capacitors in parallel do. In turn, the increased capacitance disrupts the drive signal. Additionally, with enhancement mode MOSFETs, they are always off until the gate action turns them on. Turning the I/O pin to MOSFETs on and off will result in a charge and discharge curve in the output voltage waveform, which ultimately causes the unexpected circuit behavior many witness in experiments.

visual_correlations.comment: The speaker Lewis Loflin began by explaining how the common problem of connecting MOSFETs in parallel lies in the oftentimes neglected Cgs, or capacitance gate source, which is also connected in parallel when MOSFETs are connected in parallel. As a result, the capacitance adds up as capacitors in parallel do. In turn, the increased capacitance disrupts the drive signal. Additionally, with enhancement mode MOSFETs, they are always off until the gate action turns them on. Turning the I/O pin to MOSFETs on and off will result in a charge and discharge curve in the output voltage waveform, which ultimately causes the unexpected circuit behavior many witness in experiments.
